prompt: A friend wired a 5 V strip straight to a 3.3 V GPIO and reports it has run all week. Why is that not evidence you can leave the buffer off?
options: 3.3 V sits under the pixel's worst-case 3.5 V bar, so the build is running on part-to-part slack
Their strip is shorter, and the threshold climbs as you add pixels to the chain
A GPIO driving a load outside its rating degrades over weeks, so it will fail eventually

prompt: A classmate wires a 30-pixel strip to the board's own USB 5 V, and the whole board browns out on the first full-white frame. What did they run into?
options: Voltage: a strip that long needs more than 5 V to reach its far end
Noise: USB power is too dirty for the pixel data to survive the trip
Current: about 60 mA per pixel at full white is roughly 1.8 A, past the polyfuse and past the port

prompt: The two 5 V rails must never share copper, yet the two grounds must be joined. Why is ground the exception?
options: A shared ground gives the strip a second path for its supply current, which halves the drop
The strip reads its data input as a voltage measured against its own ground, so without a shared reference the signal means nothing
Ground carries the data signal itself, so the strip receives nothing until the two are tied

prompt: The onboard pixel is sold as WS2812B compatible. What does that word actually promise you?
options: That its electrical specifications match the reference part it clones
That the manufacturer has tested it against the reference part
Only that it speaks the same protocol: its supply range and the voltage that kills its data pin are its own

prompt: You already have 10 µF parts on the reel. Why is the bulk capacitor on the USB 5 V rail specified at 4.7 µF instead?
options: USB caps a device's total bus capacitance at 10 µF, and this board already spends some of it elsewhere
A 10 µF part is too slow to answer the pixel's 60 mA current pulses
The 10 µF version of that part only comes in a package too small to hand-solder

prompt: You feed U3's VCC pin from +3V3 instead of the +5V rail. The gate still passes the signal through. What did you just undo?
options: Nothing: an AHCT output level follows its input rather than its supply
Everything: a buffer's output swings to its own supply, so the pixel is back to reading a 3.3 V high
Only the edge speed: the level still clears the pixel's bar, but the corners round off

prompt: You tie U3's 1OE pin to +5V because enable sounds like it should be high. The board powers up and the pixel stays dark. What happened?
options: The bar over 1OE means active low, so a high enable leaves that gate's output in high impedance
The gate now drives 5 V continuously, which latches the pixel at black
The gate inverts while its enable is high, so the pixel reads every bit backwards

prompt: R7 lands on the pixel's pin 2 rather than pin 4. ERC reports nothing at all. What will the built board do?
options: ERC would in fact flag it, because two outputs on one net is a pin conflict
The pixel lights, but its colours come out in the wrong order
The pixel stays dark and its own output fights the buffer, because pin 4 listens and pin 2 talks

prompt: Your ground pour spread across and joined 5V_EXT to the board's own 5 V, and DRC still passed. Why did the checker say nothing?
options: DRC only measures track widths and hole sizes, never the gap between two nets
Two nets touching is not an error unless a rule says they must stay apart, so you have to write that rule
Copper zones sit outside DRC, which checks only the traces you routed by hand

prompt: The strip's whole return current lands at J5. Why gather it into a tight via cluster there instead of letting the pour carry it away?
options: A pour is not zero resistance, and a wandering return shifts the ground your data line is measured against
A dense cluster is the only thing that ties the two inner planes to each other
KiCad will not fill a ground zone that has more than one entry point

prompt: The only board edge left for the two screw terminals is the antenna end. Why is that the wrong place, even though nothing on the board itself would move?
options: Screw terminals stand too tall to sit beside the module's body
Strip current on that edge couples straight into the USB data pair
The wires you screw into them are conductors too, and conductors near the antenna detune it

prompt: In your layout the 5 V warning text at J5 overlaps a terminal pad. What arrives on the finished boards?
options: The warning, printed over the pad exactly as you drew it
A warning with a hole in it, or none at all: fabs strip silkscreen off exposed pads automatically
Nothing changes, and DRC would have flagged the overlap before you exported

prompt: A listing reads addressable RGB LED strip, 60 pixels per metre, individually controllable, 12 V. Can you drive it from this board?
options: No: 12 V addressable strips are a different chip family, and this board's terminal is 5 V only
Yes, as long as firmware caps the brightness so the current stays low
Yes, if the strip is long enough that its far end drops back near 5 V

prompt: The lesson insists the strip's supply be fused or current-limited. What is standing behind that requirement?
options: The strip has no limit of its own, so it would draw current until the pixels burned out
USB requires it of any supply that shares a ground with the bus
The board's polyfuse cannot reach that rail, and the TVS defending it is sacrificial, so only something upstream can end a fault

prompt: A pixel pad still refuses to wet after two attempts. What is the move?
options: Turn the iron up and stay on the pad until the solder finally takes
More flux, let it cool, then a short return pass: around 315 °C and brief dwells
Switch to hot air, which heats the whole part evenly and spares the lens

prompt: Your layout passed DRC with the isolation rule loaded. Why does the meter still have to check the two 5 V rails on the built board?
options: The rule checked the design file, and a stray strand or a solder splash between two terminal pins exists only on the board you built
DRC does not examine power nets, only the signal nets you routed
It confirms the rule itself was written correctly before you order more boards

prompt: The onboard pixel is happily cycling colours, and your multimeter reads 0.4 V at TP3 on the shifted line. Is the buffer failing?
options: Yes: a working shifted line should sit near 5 V the whole time the pixel is lit
Yes: the pixel is running on luck, which is the marginal case this board exists to prevent
No: a meter reports an average and the data line spends most of its time low, so only a scope shows the peak

prompt: The strip's supply is definitely on and its current limit is pegged, yet the onboard pixel and the strip are both dark. What does that combination point at?
options: A tripped polyfuse on the USB rail, which has cut the board's own 5 V
A TVS on the external rail that has failed short, a fault with no indicator LED to announce it
Firmware that never started, so nothing is driving the data line at all
